\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:experiments}

\subsection{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:setup}

\paragraph{Models.}
We evaluate seven models spanning five architecture families and diverse attention configurations:
\textbf{Qwen2.5-7B} (GQA 7:1, 28 layers $\times$ 4 KV heads = 112),
\textbf{Qwen2.5-14B} (GQA 5:1, 48 $\times$ 8 = 384),
\textbf{Yi-1.5-9B} (GQA 8:1, 48 $\times$ 4 = 192),
\textbf{Llama-3.1-8B} (GQA 4:1, 32 $\times$ 8 = 256),
\textbf{Mistral-7B-v0.3} (GQA 4:1, 32 $\times$ 8 = 256, sliding window attention),
\textbf{Gemma-2-9B} (GQA 2:1, 42 $\times$ 8 = 336, \texttt{head\_dim}=256, attention logit softcapping),
and \textbf{Pythia-1.4B} (MHA 1:1, 24 $\times$ 16 = 384).
This selection spans GQA ratios from 1:1 (MHA) to 8:1 and covers standard, sliding-window, softcapped, and multi-head attention.

\paragraph{Evaluation.}
We report perplexity (PPL, $\downarrow$) on the WikiText-2 test split (298{,}938 tokens) under bf16 inference with stride 512.
For downstream evaluation, we use ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, PIQA, and WinoGrande under 0-shot prompting.

\paragraph{Profiling.}
Per-head sensitivity is measured by independently quantizing each head to each candidate bit-width in $\{2, 4, 8, 16\}$ and recording the PPL increase over the bf16 baseline.
All results use high-resolution profiling (64 sequences $\times$ 2048 tokens from WikiText-2 train); Appendix~\ref{sec:profiling_resolution} compares against standard-resolution profiling (16 seq $\times$ 512 tok).

\paragraph{Compression and constraint.}
The default target is 4$\times$ compression (average 4 bits, budget ratio 0.25).
The cardinality constraint limits 2-bit assignments to at most $k$ heads, where $k$ is selected via the compounding sweep described in \S\ref{sec:method} ($k{=}8$ for Qwen-7B, $k{=}2$ for Yi-1.5 and Llama, $k{=}4$ for Mistral, $k{=}8$ for Gemma-2; Qwen-14B and Pythia $k$ values pending).

\paragraph{Baselines.}
We compare against:
(1)~uniform 4-bit quantization;
(2)~unconstrained greedy allocation (RateQuant-style~\cite{zuo2026ratequant});
(3)~unconstrained MCKP allocation;
(4)~an L0-random heuristic that assigns Layer-0 heads to 8-bit and $k$ random non-Layer-0 heads to 2-bit, with remaining heads at 4-bit (5 seeds; we report mean$\pm$std and median);
and (5)~a naive positional heuristic that assigns Layer-0 to 8-bit and the $k$ deepest heads to 2-bit.

\subsection{Main Results}
\label{sec:main_results}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{PPL ($\downarrow$) on WikiText-2 at 4$\times$ compression. Unconstrained failure severity forms a three-tier gradient: \emph{catastrophic} on Qwen-7B ($3.3\times$ bf16), \emph{moderate} on Gemma-2 ($1.5\times$), \emph{mild} on the remaining models (${\sim}1.1\times$). Greedy and MCKP produce identical unconstrained allocations on 4/5 models. Best constrained result per model in \textbf{bold}; --- = experiment pending. $^\ddagger$Best $k$ from ablation ($k{=}4$). $^*$BOS-corrected.}
\label{tab:main_results}
\begin{tabular}{lccccc}
\toprule
Model & Baseline & Uniform & \multicolumn{2}{c}{Unconstrained} & Ours \\
\cmidrule(lr){4-5}
 & (bf16) & (4-bit) & Greedy & MCKP & (Constr.) \\
\midrule
Qwen2.5-7B      & 9.81  & 15.45 & 32.45 & 36.92 & \textbf{10.91} \\
Qwen2.5-14B     & 5.84  & ---   & ---   & ---   & --- \\
Yi-1.5-9B       & 7.02  & 7.22  & 7.56  & 7.56  & 7.22 \\
Llama-3.1-8B    & 8.09  & 8.47  & 8.63  & 8.63  & \textbf{8.45} \\
Mistral-7B-v0.3 & 7.04  & 7.13  & 7.57  & 7.60  & 7.16$^\ddagger$ \\
Gemma-2-9B$^*$  & 6.03  & 6.17  & 8.85  & 8.85  & 6.20 \\
Pythia-1.4B     & 13.63 & ---   & ---   & ---   & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

On Qwen2.5-7B, constrained MCKP achieves 10.91 PPL, a 29.4\% reduction over uniform 4-bit (15.45).
Without the constraint, both greedy (32.45) and MCKP (36.92) perform \emph{worse} than uniform---a catastrophic failure from excessive 2-bit assignments compounding across layers.
Across 3 calibration seeds, constrained MCKP yields mean PPL 10.99$\pm$0.06 with 90.2\% three-way allocation agreement, confirming profiling stability.

On Llama-3.1-8B, the result is essentially indistinguishable from uniform (8.45 vs.\ 8.47, $\Delta < 0.02$ PPL).
Hires profiling reveals a spike pattern (concentration 0.34, $t_1/t_5{=}0.71$) dominated by a single top head (L2H5), leaving little cross-bitwidth gradient for non-uniform allocation to exploit.

On Mistral-7B-v0.3, constrained MCKP (7.16, $k{=}4$) is slightly worse than uniform (7.13, $+$0.4\%)---a genuine negative result, as the profiler reports near-zero sensitivity differences across heads.
Mistral's sliding-window attention may contribute to this uniformity.

On Yi-1.5-9B, constrained MCKP ($k{=}2$) matches uniform at 7.22 PPL.
Despite the highest concentration tested (0.71), sensitivity is dominated by a single outlier (L4H3, $t_1/t_5{=}0.90$), a spike pattern with no cross-bitwidth gradient to exploit.

On Gemma-2-9B$^*$ (GQA 2:1), constrained MCKP ($k{=}8$) achieves 6.20 PPL vs.\ uniform 6.17, slightly above ($+$0.4\%).
Despite its flat sensitivity distribution (concentration 0.23), unconstrained MCKP degrades to 8.85 ($1.47\times$ bf16)---a moderate failure driven by the solver assigning 31.5\% of heads to 2-bit (vs.\ 4.7--16.4\% in other non-spread models).
The constraint reduces 2-bit heads from 106 to 8, confirming that it universally prevents over-allocation regardless of distribution shape.

Unconstrained failure severity forms a three-tier gradient that tracks heterogeneity shape: \emph{catastrophic} on spread-pattern Qwen ($3.3\times$ bf16), \emph{moderate} on flat-pattern Gemma-2 ($1.47\times$, driven by 31.5\% 2-bit over-allocation), and \emph{mild} on the remaining spike/flat models (${\sim}1.07$--$1.08\times$).
Greedy and MCKP produce identical unconstrained allocations on 4 of 5 models; the exception is Qwen, where MCKP assigns 7 more heads to 2-bit than greedy (75 vs.\ 68), worsening its already-catastrophic PPL.
The allocation visualization (Figure~\ref{fig:allocation}, Appendix~\ref{sec:allocation_appendix}) and budget sweep (Appendix~\ref{sec:budget_sweep}) provide additional detail.

MCKP consistently outperforms random L0-constrained allocation and naive positional baselines across all three tested models (median gap 5--16\%; Table~\ref{tab:heuristic} in Appendix~\ref{sec:heuristic_appendix}).

\paragraph{Comparison with KIVI.}
KIVI~\cite{liu2024kivi} uses asymmetric per-channel quantization with per-token scaling---a finer-grained quantization \emph{scheme} than our symmetric per-channel approach, applied uniformly across all heads.
At 4-bit with no residual channels ($r{=}0$), KIVI achieves 9.91 PPL on Qwen2.5-7B (vs.\ 9.81 bf16) and 8.14 on Llama-3.1-8B (vs.\ 8.09), both near-lossless; our symmetric uniform 4-bit yields 15.45 and 8.47, respectively.
The gap reflects the quantization scheme, not allocation strategy.
However, KIVI cannot exploit head-level heterogeneity: on Qwen (spread pattern), constrained MCKP reduces our symmetric 4-bit from 15.45 to 10.91, a $-$4.54 PPL improvement from reallocating bits across heads---a degree of freedom unavailable to any uniform-precision method.
On Llama (spike), the allocation gain is negligible ($-$0.02), consistent with the heterogeneity analysis.
At 2-bit ($r{=}0$), KIVI degrades to 13.34 on Qwen and 10.08 on Llama, as all heads---including the most sensitive---receive the same precision.
The two approaches are orthogonal: KIVI determines \emph{how} to quantize each head (asymmetric scaling), while our method determines \emph{at what precision} (bit-width selection across heads).
Composing KIVI's per-channel scheme with per-head mixed-precision allocation is a natural extension.

\subsection{Downstream Evaluation}
\label{sec:downstream}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{0-shot accuracy change (Ours $-$ Uniform, pts) at 4$\times$ compression. Qwen shows large gains; the remaining models show small degradations or neutrality, tracking PPL results.}
\label{tab:downstream}
\begin{tabular}{lccccc}
\toprule
Model & ARC-C & HS & PIQA & WG & Avg \\
\midrule
Qwen2.5-7B        & $+$3.2 & $+$4.0 & $+$1.3 & $+$2.0 & $+$2.6 \\
Yi-1.5-9B        & $-$3.2 & $-$0.6 & $-$0.3 & $+$1.3 & $-$0.8 \\
Llama-3.1-8B     & $-$2.7 & $-$0.1 & $-$0.7 & $-$0.2 & $-$1.0 \\
Mistral-7B       & $-$1.2 & $-$0.2 & $+$0.4 & $-$1.0 & $-$0.5 \\
Gemma-2-9B       & $-$0.2 & $+$0.3 & $-$0.1 & $+$0.8 & $+$0.1 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

On Qwen, constrained MCKP improves average 0-shot accuracy by 2.6 pts over uniform (0.686 vs.\ 0.660), recovering $\sim$73\% of the accuracy lost to quantization.
The four non-spread architectures show minor average degradation (Yi $-$0.8, Llama $-$1.0, Mistral $-$0.5, Gemma-2 $+$0.1 pts); Llama is the most systematic, with 0 of 5 tasks showing positive change.
ARC-Challenge shows the largest per-task sensitivity across all models (Yi $-$3.2, Llama $-$2.7, Mistral $-$1.2, Gemma-2 $-$0.2 pts), consistent with multi-step reasoning where KV cache errors accumulate across longer inference chains.
Cross-dataset stability analysis (Appendix~\ref{sec:cross_dataset}) confirms ${>}96\%$ bit-assignment agreement between WikiText-2 and C4 calibration across all three tested models.

\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:experiments}

\subsection{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:setup}

\paragraph{Models.}
We evaluate seven models spanning five architecture families and diverse attention configurations:
\textbf{Qwen2.5-7B} (GQA 7:1, 28 layers $\times$ 4 KV heads = 112),
\textbf{Qwen2.5-14B} (GQA 5:1, 48 $\times$ 8 = 384),
\textbf{Yi-1.5-9B} (GQA 8:1, 48 $\times$ 4 = 192),
\textbf{Llama-3.1-8B} (GQA 4:1, 32 $\times$ 8 = 256),
\textbf{Mistral-7B-v0.3} (GQA 4:1, 32 $\times$ 8 = 256, sliding window attention),
\textbf{Gemma-2-9B} (GQA 2:1, 42 $\times$ 8 = 336, \texttt{head\_dim}=256, attention logit softcapping),
and \textbf{Pythia-1.4B} (MHA 1:1, 24 $\times$ 16 = 384).
This selection spans GQA ratios from 1:1 (MHA) to 8:1 and covers standard, sliding-window, softcapped, and multi-head attention.

\paragraph{Evaluation.}
We report perplexity (PPL, $\downarrow$) on the WikiText-2 test split (298{,}938 tokens) under bf16 inference with stride 512.
For downstream evaluation, we use ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, PIQA, and WinoGrande under 0-shot prompting.

\paragraph{Profiling.}
Per-head sensitivity is measured by independently quantizing each head to each candidate bit-width in $\{2, 4, 8, 16\}$ and recording the PPL increase over the bf16 baseline.
All results use high-resolution profiling (64 sequences $\times$ 2048 tokens from WikiText-2 train); Appendix~\ref{sec:profiling_resolution} compares against standard-resolution profiling (16 seq $\times$ 512 tok).

\paragraph{Compression and constraint.}
The default target is 4$\times$ compression (average 4 bits, budget ratio 0.25).
The cardinality constraint limits 2-bit assignments to at most $k$ heads, where $k$ is selected via the compounding sweep described in \S\ref{sec:method} ($k{=}8$ for Qwen-7B, $k{=}2$ for Yi-1.5 and Llama, $k{=}4$ for Mistral, $k{=}8$ for Gemma-2; Qwen-14B and Pythia $k$ values pending).

\paragraph{Baselines.}
We compare against:
(1)~uniform 4-bit quantization;
(2)~unconstrained greedy allocation (RateQuant-style~\cite{zuo2026ratequant});
(3)~unconstrained MCKP allocation;
(4)~an L0-random heuristic that assigns Layer-0 heads to 8-bit and $k$ random non-Layer-0 heads to 2-bit, with remaining heads at 4-bit (5 seeds; we report mean$\pm$std and median);
and (5)~a naive positional heuristic that assigns Layer-0 to 8-bit and the $k$ deepest heads to 2-bit.

\subsection{Main Results}
\label{sec:main_results}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small

Greedy and MCKP produce identical unconstrained allocations on 4/5 models. On Qwen2.5-7B, constrained MCKP achieves 10.91 PPL, a 29.4\% reduction over uniform 4-bit (15.45).
Without the constraint, both greedy (32.45) and MCKP (36.92) perform \emph{worse} than uniform---a catastrophic failure from excessive 2-bit assignments compounding across layers.
Across 3 calibration seeds, constrained MCKP yields mean PPL 10.99$\pm$0.06 with 90.2\% three-way allocation agreement, confirming profiling stability.

On Llama-3.1-8B, the result is essentially indistinguishable from uniform (8.45 vs.\ 8.47, $\Delta < 0.02$ PPL).
Hires profiling reveals a spike pattern (concentration 0.34, $t_1/t_5{=}0.71$) dominated by a single top head (L2H5), leaving little cross-bitwidth gradient for non-uniform allocation to exploit.

On Mistral-7B-v0.3, constrained MCKP (7.16, $k{=}4$) is slightly worse than uniform (7.13, $+$0.4\%)---a genuine negative result, as the profiler reports near-zero sensitivity differences across heads.
Mistral's sliding-window attention may contribute to this uniformity.

On Yi-1.5-9B, constrained MCKP ($k{=}2$) matches uniform at 7.22 PPL.
Despite the highest concentration tested (0.71), sensitivity is dominated by a single outlier (L4H3, $t_1/t_5{=}0.90$), a spike pattern with no cross-bitwidth gradient to exploit.

On Gemma-2-9B$^*$ (GQA 2:1), constrained MCKP ($k{=}8$) achieves 6.20 PPL vs.\ uniform 6.17, slightly above ($+$0.4\%).
Despite its flat sensitivity distribution (concentration 0.23), unconstrained MCKP degrades to 8.85 ($1.47\times$ bf16)---a moderate failure driven by the solver assigning 31.5\% of heads to 2-bit (vs.\ 4.7--16.4\% in other non-spread models).
The constraint reduces 2-bit heads from 106 to 8, confirming that it universally prevents over-allocation regardless of distribution shape.

Unconstrained failure severity forms a three-tier gradient that tracks heterogeneity shape: \emph{catastrophic} on spread-pattern Qwen ($3.3\times$ bf16), \emph{moderate} on flat-pattern Gemma-2 ($1.47\times$, driven by 31.5\% 2-bit over-allocation), and \emph{mild} on the remaining spike/flat models (${\sim}1.07$--$1.08\times$).
Greedy and MCKP produce identical unconstrained allocations on 4 of 5 models; the exception is Qwen, where MCKP assigns 7 more heads to 2-bit than greedy (75 vs.\ 68), worsening its already-catastrophic PPL.
The allocation visualization (Figure~\ref{fig:allocation}, Appendix~\ref{sec:allocation_appendix}) and budget sweep (Appendix~\ref{sec:budget_sweep}) provide additional detail.

MCKP consistently outperforms random L0-constrained allocation and naive positional baselines across all three tested models (median gap 5--16\%; Table~\ref{tab:heuristic} in Appendix~\ref{sec:heuristic_appendix}).

\paragraph{Comparison with KIVI.}
KIVI~\cite{liu2024kivi} uses asymmetric per-channel quantization with per-token scaling, applied uniformly across all heads.
At 4-bit ($r{=}0$), KIVI achieves near-lossless PPL (9.91 on Qwen, 8.14 on Llama vs.\ 9.81/8.09 bf16), while our symmetric scheme yields 15.45 and 8.47---a gap from the quantization method, not allocation.

\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:experiments}

\subsection{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:setup}

\paragraph{Models.}
We evaluate seven models spanning five architecture families and diverse attention configurations:
\textbf{Qwen2.5-7B} (GQA 7:1, 28 layers $\times$ 4 KV heads = 112),
\textbf{Qwen2.5-14B} (GQA 5:1, 48 $\times$ 8 = 384),
\textbf{Yi-1.5-9B} (GQA 8:1, 48 $\times$ 4 = 192),
\textbf{Llama-3.1-8B} (GQA 4:1, 32 $\times$ 8 = 256),
\textbf{Mistral-7B-v0.3} (GQA 4:1, 32 $\times$ 8 = 256, sliding window attention),
\textbf{Gemma-2-9B} (GQA 2:1, 42 $\times$ 8 = 336, \texttt{head\_dim}=256, attention logit softcapping),
and \textbf{Pythia-1.4B} (MHA 1:1, 24 $\times$ 16 = 384).
This selection spans GQA ratios from 1:1 (MHA) to 8:1 and covers standard, sliding-window, softcapped, and multi-head attention.

\paragraph{Evaluation.}
We report perplexity (PPL, $\downarrow$) on the WikiText-2 test split (298{,}938 tokens) under bf16 inference with stride 512.
For downstream evaluation, we use ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, PIQA, and WinoGrande under 0-shot prompting.

\paragraph{Profiling.}
Per-head sensitivity is measured by independently quantizing each head to each candidate bit-width in $\{2, 4, 8, 16\}$ and recording the PPL increase over the bf16 baseline.
All results use high-resolution profiling (64 sequences $\times$ 2048 tokens from WikiText-2 train); Appendix~\ref{sec:profiling_resolution} compares against standard-resolution profiling (16 seq $\times$ 512 tok).

\paragraph{Compression and constraint.}
The default target is 4$\times$ compression (average 4 bits, budget ratio 0.25).
The cardinality constraint limits 2-bit assignments to at most $k$ heads, where $k$ is selected via the compounding sweep described in \S\ref{sec:method} ($k{=}8$ for Qwen-7B, $k{=}2$ for Yi-1.5 and Llama, $k{=}4$ for Mistral, $k{=}8$ for Gemma-2; Qwen-14B and Pythia $k$ values pending).

\paragraph{Baselines.}
We compare against:
(1)~uniform 4-bit quantization;
(2)~unconstrained greedy allocation (RateQuant-style~\cite{zuo2026ratequant});
(3)~unconstrained MCKP allocation;
(4)~an L0-random heuristic that assigns Layer-0 heads to 8-bit and $k$ random non-Layer-0 heads to 2-bit, with remaining heads at 4-bit (5 seeds; we report mean$\pm$std and median);
and (5)~a naive positional heuristic that assigns Layer-0 to 8-bit and the $k$ deepest heads to 2-bit.

\subsection{Main Results}
\label{sec:main_results}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{PPL ($\downarrow$) on WikiText-2 at 4$\times$ compression. Unconstrained failure severity forms a three-tier gradient: \emph{catastrophic} on Qwen-7B ($3.3\times$ bf16), \emph{moderate} on Gemma-2 ($1.5\times$), \emph{mild} on the remaining models (${\sim}1.1\times$). Greedy and MCKP produce identical unconstrained allocations on 4/5 models. Best constrained result per model in \textbf{bold}; --- = experiment pending. $^\ddagger$Best $k$ from ablation ($k{=}4$). $^*$BOS-corrected.}
\label{tab:main_results}
\begin{tabular}{lccccc}
\toprule
Model & Baseline & Uniform & \multicolumn{2}{c}{Unconstrained} & Ours \\
\cmidrule(lr){4-5}
 & (bf16) & (4-bit) & Greedy & MCKP & (Constr.) \\
\midrule
Qwen2.5-7B      & 9.81  & 15.45 & 32.45 & 36.92 & \textbf{10.91} \\
Qwen2.5-14B     & 5.84  & ---   & ---   & ---   & --- \\
Yi-1.5-9B       & 7.02  & 7.22  & 7.56  & 7.56  & 7.22 \\
Llama-3.1-8B    & 8.09  & 8.47  & 8.63  & 8.63  & \textbf{8.45} \\
Mistral-7B-v0.3 & 7.04  & 7.13  & 7.57  & 7.60  & 7.16$^\ddagger$ \\
Gemma-2-9B$^*$  & 6.03  & 6.17  & 8.85  & 8.85  & 6.20 \\
Pythia-1.4B     & 13.63 & ---   & ---   & ---   & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

On Qwen2.5-7B, constrained MCKP achieves 10.91 PPL, a 29.4\% reduction over uniform 4-bit (15.45).
Without the constraint, both greedy (32.45) and MCKP (36.92) perform \emph{worse} than uniform---a catastrophic failure from excessive 2-bit assignments compounding across layers.
Across 3 calibration seeds, constrained MCKP yields mean PPL 10.99$\pm$0.06 with 90.2\% three-way allocation agreement, confirming profiling stability.

On Llama-3.1-8B, the result is essentially indistinguishable from uniform (8.45 vs.\ 8.47, $\Delta < 0.02$ PPL).
Hires profiling reveals a spike pattern (concentration 0.34, $t_1/t_5{=}0.71$) dominated by a single top head (L2H5), leaving little cross-bitwidth gradient for non-uniform allocation to exploit.

On Mistral-7B-v0.3, constrained MCKP (7.16, $k{=}4$) is slightly worse than uniform (7.13, $+$0.4\%)---a genuine negative result, as the profiler reports near-zero sensitivity differences across heads.
Mistral's sliding-window attention may contribute to this uniformity.

On Yi-1.5-9B, constrained MCKP ($k{=}2$) matches uniform at 7.22 PPL.
Despite the highest concentration tested (0.71), sensitivity is dominated by a single outlier (L4H3, $t_1/t_5{=}0.90$), a spike pattern with no cross-bitwidth gradient to exploit.

On Gemma-2-9B$^*$ (GQA 2:1), constrained MCKP ($k{=}8$) achieves 6.20 PPL vs.\ uniform 6.17, slightly above ($+$0.4\%).
Despite its flat sensitivity distribution (concentration 0.23), unconstrained MCKP degrades to 8.85 ($1.47\times$ bf16)---a moderate failure driven by the solver assigning 31.5\% of heads to 2-bit (vs.\ 4.7--16.4\% in other non-spread models).
The constraint reduces 2-bit heads from 106 to 8, confirming that it universally prevents over-allocation regardless of distribution shape.

Unconstrained failure severity forms a three-tier gradient that tracks heterogeneity shape: \emph{catastrophic} on spread-pattern Qwen ($3.3\times$ bf16), \emph{moderate} on flat-pattern Gemma-2 ($1.47\times$, driven by 31.5\% 2-bit over-allocation), and \emph{mild} on the remaining spike/flat models (${\sim}1.07$--$1.08\times$).
See Appendix~\ref{sec:allocation_appendix} (allocation visualization) and Appendix~\ref{sec:budget_sweep} (budget sweep) for additional detail.

MCKP consistently outperforms random L0-constrained allocation and naive positional baselines across all three tested models (median gap 5--16\%; Table~\ref{tab:heuristic} in Appendix~\ref{sec:heuristic_appendix}).

\paragraph{Comparison with KIVI.}
KIVI~\cite{liu2024kivi} uses asymmetric per-channel quantization with per-token scaling, applied uniformly across all heads.
At 4-bit ($r{=}0$), KIVI achieves near-lossless PPL (9.91 on Qwen, 8.14 on Llama vs.\ 9.81/8.09 bf16), while our symmetric scheme yields 15.45 and 8.47---a gap from the quantization method, not allocation.
However, KIVI cannot exploit head-level heterogeneity: on Qwen (spread), constrained MCKP reduces symmetric 4-bit from 15.45 to 10.91 ($-$4.54 PPL) by reallocating bits across heads, a degree of freedom unavailable to uniform-precision methods; on Llama (spike), the gain is negligible ($-$0.02).
At 2-bit ($r{=}0$), KIVI degrades to 13.34 on Qwen and 10.08 on Llama, as all heads---including sensitive ones---receive the same precision.
The two approaches are orthogonal---KIVI selects the per-channel quantization scheme, our method selects the per-head bit-width---and can be composed.

\label{sec:downstream}

\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:experiments}

\subsection{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:setup}

\paragraph{Models.}
We evaluate seven models spanning five architecture families and diverse attention configurations:
\textbf{Qwen2.5-7B} (GQA 7:1, 28 layers $\times$ 4 KV heads = 112),
\textbf{Qwen2.5-14B} (GQA 5:1, 48 $\times$ 8 = 384),
\textbf{Yi-1.5-9B} (GQA 8:1, 48 $\times$ 4 = 192),
\textbf{Llama-3.1-8B} (GQA 4:1, 32 $\times$ 8 = 256),
\textbf{Mistral-7B-v0.3} (GQA 4:1, 32 $\times$ 8 = 256, sliding window attention),
\textbf{Gemma-2-9B} (GQA 2:1, 42 $\times$ 8 = 336, \texttt{head\_dim}=256, attention logit softcapping),
and \textbf{Pythia-1.4B} (MHA 1:1, 24 $\times$ 16 = 384).
This selection spans GQA ratios from 1:1 (MHA) to 8:1 and covers standard, sliding-window, softcapped, and multi-head attention.

\paragraph{Evaluation.}
We report perplexity (PPL, $\downarrow$) on the WikiText-2 test split (298{,}938 tokens) under bf16 inference with stride 512.
For downstream evaluation, we use ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, PIQA, and WinoGrande under 0-shot prompting.

\paragraph{Profiling.}
Per-head sensitivity is measured by independently quantizing each head to each candidate bit-width in $\{2, 4, 8, 16\}$ and recording the PPL increase over the bf16 baseline.
All results use high-resolution profiling (64 sequences $\times$ 2048 tokens from WikiText-2 train); Appendix~\ref{sec:profiling_resolution} compares against standard-resolution profiling (16 seq $\times$ 512 tok).

\paragraph{Compression and constraint.}
The default target is 4$\times$ compression (average 4 bits, budget ratio 0.25).
The cardinality constraint limits 2-bit assignments to at most $k$ heads, where $k$ is selected via the compounding sweep described in \S\ref{sec:method} ($k{=}8$ for Qwen-7B, $k{=}2$ for Yi-1.5 and Llama, $k{=}4$ for Mistral, $k{=}8$ for Gemma-2; Qwen-14B and Pythia $k$ values pending).

\paragraph{Baselines.}
We compare against:
(1)~uniform 4-bit quantization;
(2)~unconstrained greedy allocation (RateQuant-style~\cite{zuo2026ratequant});
(3)~unconstrained MCKP allocation;
(4)~an L0-random heuristic that assigns Layer-0 heads to 8-bit and $k$ random non-Layer-0 heads to 2-bit, with remaining heads at 4-bit (5 seeds; we report mean$\pm$std and median);
and (5)~a naive positional heuristic that assigns Layer-0 to 8-bit and the $k$ deepest heads to 2-bit.

\subsection{Main Results}
\label{sec:main_results}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{PPL ($\downarrow$) on WikiText-2 at 4$\times$ compression. Unconstrained failure severity forms a three-tier gradient: \emph{catastrophic} on Qwen-7B ($3.3\times$ bf16), \emph{moderate} on Gemma-2 ($1.5\times$), \emph{mild} on the remaining models (${\sim}1.1\times$). Greedy and MCKP produce identical unconstrained allocations on 4/5 models. Best constrained result per model in \textbf{bold}; --- = experiment pending. $^\ddagger$Best $k$ from ablation ($k{=}4$). $^*$BOS-corrected.}
\label{tab:main_results}
\begin{tabular}{lccccc}
\toprule
Model & Baseline & Uniform & \multicolumn{2}{c}{Unconstrained} & Ours \\
\cmidrule(lr){4-5}
 & (bf16) & (4-bit) & Greedy & MCKP & (Constr.) \\
\midrule
Qwen2.5-7B      & 9.81  & 15.45 & 32.45 & 36.92 & \textbf{10.91} \\
Qwen2.5-14B     & 5.84  & ---   & ---   & ---   & --- \\
Yi-1.5-9B       & 7.02  & 7.22  & 7.56  & 7.56  & 7.22 \\
Llama-3.1-8B    & 8.09  & 8.47  & 8.63  & 8.63  & \textbf{8.45} \\
Mistral-7B-v0.3 & 7.04  & 7.13  & 7.57  & 7.60  & 7.16$^\ddagger$ \\
Gemma-2-9B$^*$  & 6.03  & 6.17  & 8.85  & 8.85  & 6.20 \\
Pythia-1.4B     & 13.63 & ---   & ---   & ---   & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

On Qwen2.5-7B, constrained MCKP achieves 10.91 PPL, a 29.4\% reduction over uniform 4-bit (15.45).
Without the constraint, both greedy (32.45) and MCKP (36.92) perform \emph{worse} than uniform---a catastrophic failure from excessive 2-bit assignments compounding across layers.
Across 3 calibration seeds, constrained MCKP yields mean PPL 10.99$\pm$0.06 with 90.2\% three-way allocation agreement, confirming profiling stability.

On Llama-3.1-8B, the result is essentially indistinguishable from uniform (8.45 vs.\ 8.47, $\Delta < 0.02$ PPL).
Hires profiling reveals a spike pattern (concentration 0.34, $t_1/t_5{=}0.71$) dominated by a single top head (L2H5), leaving little cross-bitwidth gradient for non-uniform allocation to exploit.

On Mistral-7B-v0.3, constrained MCKP (7.16, $k{=}4$) is slightly worse than uniform (7.13, $+$0.4\%)---a genuine negative result, as the profiler reports near-zero sensitivity differences across heads.
Mistral's sliding-window attention may contribute to this uniformity.

On Yi-1.5-9B, constrained MCKP ($k{=}2$) matches uniform at 7.22 PPL.
Despite the highest concentration tested (0.71), sensitivity is dominated by a single outlier (L4H3, $t_1/t_5{=}0.90$), a spike pattern with no cross-bitwidth gradient to exploit.

On Gemma-2-9B$^*$ (GQA 2:1), constrained MCKP ($k{=}8$) achieves 6.20 PPL vs.\ uniform 6.17, slightly above ($+$0.4\%).
Despite its flat sensitivity distribution (concentration 0.23), unconstrained MCKP degrades to 8.85 ($1.47\times$ bf16)---a moderate failure driven by the solver assigning 31.5\% of heads to 2-bit (vs.\ 4.7--16.4\% in other non-spread models).
The constraint reduces 2-bit heads from 106 to 8, confirming that it universally prevents over-allocation regardless of distribution shape.

Unconstrained failure severity forms a three-tier gradient that tracks heterogeneity shape: \emph{catastrophic} on spread-pattern Qwen ($3.3\times$ bf16), \emph{moderate} on flat-pattern Gemma-2 ($1.47\times$, driven by 31.5\% 2-bit over-allocation), and \emph{mild} on the remaining spike/flat models (${\sim}1.07$--$1.08\times$).
See Appendix~\ref{sec:allocation_appendix} (allocation visualization) and Appendix~\ref{sec:budget_sweep} (budget sweep) for additional detail.

MCKP consistently outperforms random L0-constrained allocation and naive positional baselines across all three tested models (median gap 5--16\%; Table~\ref{tab:heuristic} in Appendix~\ref{sec:heuristic_appendix}).

\paragraph{Comparison with KIVI.}
KIVI~\cite{liu2024kivi} uses asymmetric per-channel quantization with per-token scaling, applied uniformly across all heads.
At 4-bit ($r{=}0$), KIVI achieves near-lossless PPL (9.91 on Qwen, 8.14 on Llama vs.\ 9.81/8.09 bf16), while our symmetric scheme yields 15.45 and 8.47---a gap from the quantization method, not allocation.
However, KIVI cannot exploit head-level heterogeneity: on Qwen (spread), constrained MCKP reduces symmetric 4-bit from 15.45 to 10.91 ($-$4.54 PPL) by reallocating bits across heads, a degree of freedom unavailable to uniform-precision methods; on Llama (spike), the gain is negligible ($-$0.02).
At 2-bit ($r{=}0$), KIVI degrades further (13.34 on Qwen, 10.08 on Llama) as sensitive heads receive the same precision as insensitive ones.
The two approaches are orthogonal and composable: KIVI selects the per-channel scheme, our method selects the per-head bit-width.

\subsection{Downstream Evaluation}
\label{sec:downstream}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{0-shot accuracy change (Ours $-$ Uniform, pts) at 4$\times$ compression. Qwen shows large gains; the remaining models show small degradations or neutrality, tracking PPL results.}
\label{tab:downstream}
\begin{tabular}{lccccc}
\toprule
Model & ARC-C & HS & PIQA & WG & Avg \\
\midrule
Qwen2.5-7B        & $+$3.2 & $+$4.0 & $+$1.3 & $+$2.0 & $+$2.6 \\
Yi-1.5-9B        & $-$3.2 & $-$0.6 & $-$0.3 & $+$1.3 & $-$0.8 \\
Llama-3.1-8B     & $-$2.7 & $-$0.1 & $-$0.7 & $-$0.2 & $-$1.0 \\
Mistral-7B       & $-$1.2 & $-$0.2 & $+$0.4 & $-$1.0 & $-$0.5 \\
Gemma-2-9B       & $-$0.2 & $+$0.3 & $-$0.1 & $+$0.8 & $+$0.1 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

On Qwen, constrained MCKP improves average 0-shot accuracy by 2.6 pts over uniform (0.686 vs.\ 0.660), recovering $\sim$73\% of the accuracy lost to quantization.
The four non-spread architectures show minor average degradation (Yi $-$0.8, Llama $-$1.0, Mistral $-$0.5, Gemma-2 $+$0.1 pts); Llama is the most systematic, with 0 of 5 tasks showing positive change.
ARC-Challenge shows the largest per-task sensitivity across all models (Yi $-$3.2, Llama $-$2.7, Mistral $-$1.2, Gemma-2 $-$0.2 pts), consistent with multi-step reasoning where KV cache errors accumulate across longer inference chains.
Cross-dataset stability analysis (Appendix~\ref{sec:cross_dataset}) confirms ${>}96\%$ bit-assignment agreement between WikiText-2 and C4 calibration across all three tested models.

\section{Analysis}
\label{sec:analysis}

\subsection{Heterogeneity Characterization}
\label{sec:heterogeneity}

The benefit of non-uniform allocation depends on how unevenly head sensitivities are distributed.
We quantify this with a \emph{top-5\% concentration metric}: sort per-head 2-bit distortions $d_h(2)$ in descending order and compute the fraction of total distortion contributed by the top 5\% of heads.
High concentration indicates that a few heads are disproportionately sensitive; low concentration indicates near-uniform sensitivity.

Table~\ref{tab:heterogeneity} summarizes the results across seven models at $4\times$ compression.
The central finding is that MCKP benefit requires \emph{spread heterogeneity}---multiple heads with cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradients---rather than sensitivity concentrated in a single outlier at one bitwidth.

Qwen2.5-7B exemplifies the spread pattern (top-5\% concentration 0.61, $t_1/t_5{=}0.57$), with Layer-0 heads contributing the majority of total 2-bit distortion across multiple bitwidths.
Constrained MCKP reduces degradation from $+$5.64 PPL (uniform) to $+$1.10 PPL, a 29.4\% improvement over uniform 4-bit. %exp_id=qwen_constrained_mckp

Yi-1.5-9B is a critical counterexample: despite the highest concentration tested ($0.71$, exceeding Qwen's $0.61$), constrained MCKP matches uniform ($+$0.20 vs.\ $+$0.20). %exp_id=yi15_hires_constrained_mckp
Yi-1.5's sensitivity is dominated by a single extreme outlier: Layer-4 Head-3 ($d_h(2){=}13.12$, second-ranked head: $0.55$, a $24\times$ gap; $t_1/t_5{=}0.90$). %exp_id=yi15_hires_profiling
Critically, L4H3's 4-bit and 8-bit deltas are ${\approx}\,0$, so upgrading it from 2-bit to 4-bit removes the distortion, but budget freed by downgrading other heads has nowhere useful to go---a ``spike'' pattern with sensitivity at only one bitwidth.
In contrast, Qwen's Layer-0 heads exhibit non-zero deltas at multiple bitwidths (e.g., L0H0: 2-bit delta ${=}6.74$, with positive 4-bit and 8-bit deltas), giving the solver a multi-bitwidth gradient across several heads---a ``spread'' pattern enabling meaningful reallocation. %exp_id=qwen_hires_profiling

Llama-3.1-8B shows moderate concentration ($0.34$) with a spike pattern ($t_1/t_5{=}0.71$); its allocation is indistinguishable from uniform ($+$0.36 vs.\ $+$0.38). %exp_id=llama_hires_bf16_2bitonly %exp_id=llama_hires_constrained
Mistral-7B-v0.3 ($t_1/t_5{=}0.18$) and Gemma-2-9B ($t_1/t_5{=}0.18$) both exhibit flat distributions with low concentration ($0.22$ and $0.23$), leaving no reliable signal; constrained MCKP is slightly worse than uniform in both cases ($+$0.13 vs.\ $+$0.10 for Mistral; $+$0.16 vs.\ $+$0.14 for Gemma-2). %exp_id=mistral_c4_cross_dataset %exp_id=gemma2_full_pipeline

Pythia-1.4B extends the evaluation to MHA (1:1 ratio, 384 heads).
Despite a moderately elevated $t_1/t_5$ ratio ($1.94$), its low concentration ($0.24$) places it in the flat category: with $3.4\times$ more heads than Qwen-7B, individual sensitivities are diluted below the threshold where any single outlier can drive meaningful reallocation.
Sensitivity clusters in mid-layer heads (L1, L8--L17) rather than Layer-0, confirming that MHA architectures follow the same concentration-driven logic as GQA.

\paragraph{Scale-dependent concentration dilution.}
Qwen2.5-14B (GQA 5:1, 384 heads) provides a within-family comparison: concentration drops from 0.61 (7B) to 0.33 (14B), and $t_1/t_5$ rises from 0.57 to 0.68---a transition from spread to flat.
Sensitivity is dominated by a single head (L0H5, $d_h(2){=}1.845$; second-ranked: $0.237$, a $7.8\times$ gap), while the $3.4\times$ increase in head count ($112{\to}384$) dilutes the remaining signal below the concentration threshold.
Spread heterogeneity is thus not an intrinsic property of an architecture family but depends on scale: the rule correctly identifies Qwen-7B as the single model$\times$scale combination where non-uniform allocation helps.

\centering
\small
\caption{Head sensitivity heterogeneity and constrained allocation benefit at $4\times$ compression. $t_1/t_5$: ratio of top-1 to top-5 per-head 2-bit distortion (low${=}$spread, high${=}$spike). --- = experiment pending. $^*$BOS-corrected.}
\label{tab:heterogeneity}
\begin{tabular}{lcccccc}
\toprule
Model & GQA & Top-5\% & $t_1/t_5$ & $\Delta$ PPL & $\Delta$ PPL & Shape \\
 & Ratio & Conc. & & (Uniform) & (Ours) & \\
\midrule
Qwen2.5-7B & 7:1 & 0.61 & 0.57 & $+$5.64 & $+$1.10 & Spread \\
Qwen2.5-14B & 5:1 & 0.33 & 0.68 & --- & --- & Flat \\
Yi-1.5-9B & 8:1 & 0.71 & 0.90 & $+$0.20 & $+$0.20 & Spike \\
Llama-3.1-8B & 4:1 & 0.34 & 0.71 & $+$0.38 & $+$0.36 & Spike \\
Mistral-7B-v0.3 & 4:1 & 0.22 & 0.18 & $+$0.10 & $+$0.13 & Flat \\
Gemma-2-9B$^*$ & 2:1 & 0.23 & 0.18 & $+$0.14 & $+$0.16 & Flat \\
Pythia-1.4B & 1:1 & 0.24 & 1.94 & --- & --- & Flat \\

The per-head heatmap (Figure~\ref{fig:heatmap}, Appendix~\ref{sec:heatmap_appendix}) confirms this visually: Qwen's Layer-0 heads show high distortion while mid-to-deep layers are near-zero (spread); Yi-1.5 shows a single bright spot at Layer-4 Head-3 (34\% of total delta) with the remaining 191 heads near-uniform (spike); Gemma-2 and Mistral show uniformly low distortion.

\subsection{Empirical Decision Rule}
\label{sec:diagnostic}

MCKP benefit requires not just high concentration but a specific \emph{shape}---spread heterogeneity across multiple heads with cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradients.
This motivates a joint empirical decision rule for deciding when non-uniform allocation is worthwhile.
Given the profiling results from \S\ref{sec:profiling}, compute the top-5\% concentration and $t_1/t_5$ ratio, then select:
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
\item \textbf{Spread} (concentration $\gtrsim 0.50$, $t_1/t_5 \lesssim 0.70$): non-uniform recommended. Qwen (0.61, $t_1/t_5{=}0.57$): $-$29.4\% PPL.
\item \textbf{Spike} ($t_1/t_5 \gtrsim 0.70$, concentration $\gtrsim 0.25$): use uniform. A dominant outlier with no cross-bitwidth gradient cannot be exploited. Yi-1.5 (0.71, 0.90) and Llama (0.34, 0.71): no benefit.
\item \textbf{Flat} (concentration $\lesssim 0.25$, or remaining moderate-concentration models with $t_1/t_5 \lesssim 0.70$): use uniform. Too little cumulative delta for meaningful reallocation. Mistral (0.22), Gemma-2 (0.23), Qwen-14B (0.33), and Pythia (0.24): no benefit or counterproductive.
\end{itemize}

Per-head mixed-precision KV cache quantization over hardware-aligned bit-widths \{2, 4, 8, 16\} requires a cardinality constraint on 2-bit assignments to prevent non-additive distortion compounding.
On Qwen2.5-7B, limiting 2-bit heads to $k{\leq}8$ reduces PPL from 15.45 (uniform 4-bit) to 10.91 ($-$29.4\%) at $4\times$ compression, while making solver choice irrelevant: constrained greedy and MCKP produce identical allocations across all tested architectures.
